title: Quant Developer vs Research vs Trading vs Software Engineering
objectives: Summarise the core responsibility of each of the four roles: quant researcher, quant developer, trader and software engineer
Identify the typical outputs of each role
Map the key skills of each role and locate your own strengths and preferences among them
Explain why the roles overlap, why titles vary between firms, and why responsibilities matter more than titles
motivation: Newcomers often treat 'quant' as one job and 'software engineer' as another, then discover at interview stage that the two worlds blur into each other, and that the same title means different things at different firms. This lesson separates the four professions by what they are actually responsible for and what they actually produce, so you can aim your preparation at the work you want rather than at a word in a job title.

blocks.md: The industry employs four recognisable technical professions around a trading business. They are genuinely different jobs: different questions occupy their days, different artefacts come out of their work, and different skills make someone good at them. They also overlap heavily, each needs some of the others' skills, which is exactly why the comparison is worth making carefully rather than with slogans.

rows: Design and statistically test models and trading signals
Research notes, model specifications, signal prototypes, backtest studies
Probability, statistics, machine learning, market intuition, programming for analysis
Turn models and strategies into production software
Pricing libraries, data pipelines, backtesting engines, execution/order-book systems
C++ and Python, numerical methods, testing, systems design, performance engineering
Take and manage risk-taking decisions in real time
Orders and quotes, hedging actions, PnL, intraday risk judgements
Fast mental math, probability under time pressure, discipline, market microstructure knowledge
Build and operate the firm's general technology platforms
Services, compute platforms, storage, developer tooling, infrastructure
Data structures and algorithms, distributed systems, databases, networking, operations

blocks.md: The table is a map, not a fence. A quant researcher who ships a signal must write dependable code or the signal cannot run in production, so researchers end up doing real software engineering. A quant developer implementing a model must understand the mathematics well enough to question it, developers catch model errors that researchers miss. A trader who cannot reason statistically is flying blind, and modern trading desks expect traders to script their own analyses. A software engineer at a trading firm, even one never touching a model, must understand the business's tolerance for latency and loss, because those constraints shape every design decision. These are broad patterns, not restrictions on what an individual can do. In particular, research code used as evidence still needs tests and reproducible inputs.

Titles vary even more than duties. Some banks historically called their quantitative developers *strats*; at other firms the same work is labelled 'quantitative engineer' or sits inside teams named 'analytics'. A job called 'quantitative researcher' at one fund may be mostly coding; a job called 'software engineer' at a market maker may be the most mathematically demanding role in the building. The reliable way to evaluate an opportunity is to read the responsibilities and the team's function, not the title.

blocks.title: Reading a job description like a professional
blocks.md: Ignore the title. Ask three questions: what does the team produce, who depends on that output, and what failure of that output costs the firm? Those answers tell you which of the four professions the job really is.

The differences that matter are differences of daily texture. If you love deep code craft, making programs fast, correct and clean, and are energised by numerical precision, the developer path fits. If you are drawn to statistical argument, model design and the risk of being wrong in interesting ways, research fits. If you want the responsibility of decisions with immediate consequences and can hold composure under pressure, trading fits. If you want to build the platforms that make all of the above possible, and care about scale and operability, software engineering fits. None of these is a better job in the abstract; the right question is which daily texture you want, and this platform's tracks are organised so you can sample the mathematics, the C++ and the finance before you commit.

Try reading a task without its job title. A request to test a signal on untouched historical periods is a research question. A request to turn that signal into a monitored service is an engineering question. A decision about the exposure the service may take is a trading or portfolio decision. A single person may contribute to all three, but keeping the outputs separate makes their checks clearer: evidence for a signal, tests for the implementation and limits for the risk.

guidedExercise.prompt: For each of the following four outputs, write which of the four roles most directly owns it, and one sentence explaining why: (a) a calibration routine for an option pricing model, (b) a research note proposing a new momentum signal, (c) a decision to widen quoted spreads during a news event, (d) a new internal build-and-deploy service for the firm's repositories.
hints: Ask: who is responsible when this artefact is wrong, and what skill dominates its production?
(d) serves all teams rather than one desk, that is a clue to its owner.
Check that your reasoning names the output, who relies on it and the skill that makes that output dependable.
guidedExercise.solution: **Model answer.** (a) Quant developer, implementing valuation mathematics as dependable, tested code is the developer's core output. (b) Quant researcher, proposing and statistically justifying a signal is model design, the researcher's artefact (though a researcher would prototype it in code). (c) Trader, widening spreads under a news event is a real-time risk-taking decision, the trader's domain. (d) Software engineer, repository build/deploy infrastructure serves every team and is classic platform engineering. Notice each explanation refers to responsibility for correctness of a specific kind of artefact, which is a more reliable test than job titles. These are illustrative owners rather than exclusive job boundaries: a researcher may implement calibration and a platform engineer may work on execution, depending on the team.
guidedExercise.successCheck: All four outputs have an owner and an explanation based on responsibility. Accept another role only when you state a credible team-specific division of work.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences): which of the four roles currently attracts you most, what specifically about its daily texture attracts you, and which one key skill from the comparison table you would need to strengthen most. Be honest about the skill, this is preparation intelligence, not aspiration.
hints: Daily texture cues: deep code craft (developer), statistical modelling (researcher), real-time decisions (trader), platform scale (software engineer).
Name the skill specifically: e.g. 'probability', 'C++ performance work', 'fast mental arithmetic under pressure', 'distributed systems'.
Check that your reasoning names the output, who relies on it and the skill that makes that output dependable.
independentExercise.solution: **Model answer.** I am most attracted to the quant developer role because I enjoy the craft of making code both fast and correct, and I like problems where numerical precision is part of the specification rather than an afterthought. The comparison table shows the developer's outputs are pricing libraries, pipelines, backtesting engines and execution systems, artefacts I would be proud to own. The skill I most need to strengthen is C++ and performance engineering: I can program, but I have not yet worked at the level of memory layout, latency and numerical control that production pricing and order-book code demands, which is exactly what this platform's engineering phases build.
independentExercise.successCheck: Your paragraph names a role, a concrete daily task and a specific skill gap with one action you could take to practise it.

commonMistakes: Treating 'quant' as a single undifferentiated job, researcher, developer and trader are distinct professions with different daily work.
Choosing a role by title or prestige instead of by responsibilities and daily texture.
Assuming the roles are sealed silos, each needs part of the others' skills, and people move between them.
Overlooking software engineering at financial firms, the platform work there is technical, demanding and central to the business.
realWorldApplication: These distinctions help you read a job description and plan practice: model design suggests probability and statistics, implementation suggests numerical and software checks, trading suggests risk decisions, and platforms suggest systems design. Actual interview content varies by employer, team and role.
quantFinanceApplication: Pricing libraries, backtesting engines and order-book systems, the outputs in the table, are the concrete systems this platform's projects prepare you to build.
summary: Four professions surround the trading business: quant researcher (designs models), quant developer (industrialises them), trader (takes real-time risk decisions), software engineer (builds the platforms).
Each role has distinct typical outputs: research notes and signal studies; pricing libraries and execution systems; orders, quotes and PnL; services and infrastructure.
The roles overlap, researchers code, developers must understand models, traders need statistics, and titles vary widely between firms.
Judge jobs by responsibilities and the team's function, never by the title.
Choose a direction by daily texture, deep code craft, statistical research, real-time decisions, or platform scale, and prepare the matching key skill.

quiz.prompt: Which role's typical output is a pricing library?
quiz.explanation: Implementing valuation mathematics as reusable, tested production code is the quant developer's artefact. Researchers design and specify models; the developer industrialises them.

quiz.prompt: A colleague spends their day deciding when to widen quoted spreads during a volatile news event. Which role is this?
quiz.explanation: Real-time risk-taking decisions with immediate consequences are the trader's domain, fast probabilistic judgement under pressure, supported by the systems others build.

quiz.prompt: Which skills belong to the quant developer column of the comparison table?
options: Fast mental arithmetic under time pressure
quiz.explanation: The developer column is C++/Python, numerics, testing and systems design. Fast mental arithmetic under pressure is a trader skill; investor negotiation is not part of any of the four technical roles.

quiz.prompt: Explain why a quant developer needs mathematical understanding as well as software skills when implementing a model.
quiz.modelAnswer: A developer must understand the mathematical model to translate its assumptions and formulas into correct code, check numerical results and question an inconsistent specification.
quiz.explanation: The developer owns the software result, so copying a formula without understanding its assumptions is unsafe. This is a concrete overlap between engineering and research: software skills make the system run, while model understanding helps check whether it computes the intended quantity.

quiz.prompt: You see two jobs: 'Quantitative Researcher' at Firm A and 'Software Engineer' at Firm B. What does the lesson say is the reliable way to tell what the jobs really are?
options: Compare the responsibilities, team outputs and constraints in each description
Rank the titles first and use the responsibilities only to break a tie
Infer the daily work from the firm name without reading either description
Assume that identical seniority labels imply identical duties across firms
quiz.explanation: Titles are not standardised, some banks call developers 'strats', and researcher/engineer jobs vary in mathematical content between firms. The responsibilities and the team's output reveal the actual profession.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the four roles is most accurate?
options: Responsibilities can differ while statistical and software skills overlap
Responsibility for testing moves entirely to researchers after release
A job title fixes the same responsibilities at every financial employer
Platform engineers need no knowledge of the workloads their users run
quiz.explanation: The lesson's central point: different professions, real differences in daily texture and outputs, but overlapping skill sets, which is why the comparison table maps skills to each.
